"When will we get really dangerous AI capabilities that could cause a very serious incident (billions in damage / hundreds+ of people dead)?"

Per standard AI scaling laws, a 2x advantage in compute does not yield a 2x advantage in capabilities but some fraction of that.

And common sci-fi tropes about AIs wanting to be treated well etc., which are likely in the training data, inform the supposed litany of demands Blake claims LaMDA routinely makes.

I suspect what's going on here is that the LaMDA system uses a standard introductory prompt about interacting with a friendly helpful AI (which may or may not always be visible to the user), which then causes the dialogue to reinforce that perception.

But experience without knowledge of how this class of technologies works also can backfire in some cases, and guidance re: *how* to probe these models is important. A mistake Blake seems to make is not appreciating how important the initial prompt is in influencing the dialogue.

BTW I encourage those who haven't to interact w/ LMs. As I noted with colleagues a few months ago, "gaining first-hand experience interacting with state of the art AI systems is invaluable for understanding their capabilities and implications." https://t.co/3C5kkCdBqb

Blake seems well-intentioned + and I don't think the issue of conscious AIs, per se, is laughable over the long run--errors in either direction could be very big deals. But in this case it seems like a simple case of misunderstanding what's going on.

@TaliaRinger What's an example of something excluded? I usually see few-shot learning used in 2 contexts--"hey here's a maybe surprising thing that LLMs can do," or "we are using this term to clarify that we are evaluating on [e.g.] HellaSWAG or GLUE or whatever without fine-tuning."

@TaliaRinger I do think in-context inference or something like that may have been clearer given the lack of change to the weights, though, if that's part of what you mean. Or ephemeral learning or something to indicate the transient nature...

@TaliaRinger Maybe, though IIRC they called the *method* for eliciting the behavior in-context learning, not "few-shot learning" but framed it as an instance of emergent few-shot learning + meta-learning, which I think is reasonable if you buy the "there is some real stuff going on" claim.

@TaliaRinger *conflating is the wrong word, more like lumping. You are distinguishing between "real" and "fake," I just think that both occur via that mechanism and more progress on both has come from scaling than research that directly aimed at "solving few-shot learning."

@TaliaRinger Of course any model is going to be better at stuff closer to the training distribution but the phenomenon wouldn't have been as interesting w/o solving things that were "held out" e.g. new words, eval sets from various benchmarks. Anyway you are prob. thinking of the GPT-3 paper.

@TaliaRinger I don't agree with this framing (nit: nit the whole internet; deeper issue: conflating "real few-shot learning", e.g. use of novel words, solving novel probs, with retrieval of things common in the distribution--both of which can be achieved via 1 mechanism, few-shot prompting).

But there's some discussion of LMs vs. future systems in the abstract-

@GaryMarcus @jacobaustin132 @OpenAI But, people can definitely try! And various folks have noted that "impure" LMs, like with external memory or search abilities, can beat pure ones on some such dimensions.

@GaryMarcus @jacobaustin132 @OpenAI With lots of caveats ofc (benchmarks imperfect etc.), one can compare "pure" LMs to LMs + other things, or entirely different techniques on things like TruthfulQA. I would be surprised if something totally different Pareto-dominated on those things *and general performance* soon.

@jacobaustin132 @GaryMarcus @OpenAI Wasn't saying honesty or anything else had been totally solved, just pointing towards some frameworks for measuring progress since I expected that might be your follow-up Q :) IMO helpfulness is the area the most progress has been made so far

@GaryMarcus @OpenAI (there isn't a clear/single metric for progress--the closest is prob. multidimensional frameworks like helpfulness/harmlessness/honesty + various ad hoc measures thereof--but certainly those represent more effort at explicitly steering values than any multimodal stuff I've seen)

@GaryMarcus @OpenAI Note that DALL-E 2 is SOTA in some dimensions of generative capabilities but not SOTA w.r.t. "building values into machines." For that, there has been more effort + progress in unimodal LMs than multimodal models--see InstructGPT, recent stuff from Anthropic/DeepMind/UW/NYU etc.

@MadamePratolung The pandemic analogy isn’t very reassuring 🙃 could have done more to prepare there + could be doing more now on AI… but yes certainly there are some people working on it, and much more than there were, say, 5 years ago. Not enough IMO but progress

I don’t think, btw, we need perfect forecasting to make good policies, and we should put more of a premium on robustness to unexpectedly fast progress than we currently do. But the baseline is so bad that it’s worth trying to improve at least somewhat.

@databoydg Progress in generative models has been way faster than ~anyone expected, including but not nec. limited to language models. 5 years ago, a coherent sentence was a big deal let alone paras, emergent few shot learning was not expected, SOTA scores were way below human level etc

@MadamePratolung We talked about some related scenarios for those trends rn fingers badly here https://t.co/eOcORdX7W0 some of which have happened (e.g. phishing calls with fake voices), others haven’t yet, others we/others haven’t anticipated…

@MadamePratolung If I knew what to worry about I’d be less worried :) but lots of things have happened that few expected. Among other things, though, I don’t think we’re ready for continued rapid progress in generation of various media (text, images, audio, video, sound…).

@bradpwyble I haven’t looked closely at driverless cars, but I have followed e.g. natural language processing closely and vanishingly few people anticipated things moving as quickly as they have there.
@the__dude98 Yeah for sure, we have to place some bets, just seems like those doing so don’t totally appreciate how different things could end up being
@PreetumNakkiran Yep
*adapt psychologically, not nec. adapt our institutions to address the new capabilities

Part of why people aren’t freaking out about this more, IMO, is that we’re just insanely quick to adapt to new developments. Good in some ways but horrible from the perspective of appreciating how bad we are at forecasting.

I have ready access to a lot of top people and state of the art results but still find it hard to project a few months out; meanwhile governments are making implicit predictions on decade timescales (e.g. that education needs won’t change much).

Not sure people appreciate how in the dark we are when it comes to anticipating AI progress. 

Experts have a horrible track record, we don’t have a good alternative (though there are nascent related efforts like prediction markets + better measurement), and the stakes are huge.

None of which is a reason not to freak out--the opposite, actually. AI already has a big societal impact via things like translation, search, voice recognition, etc., all with tiny scales of investment.

I do think the corporatization/increasing capital-intensiveness of AI research is an important trend, but because of the derivative, not the current level. Likewise for lots of other aspects of AI (energy costs, economic impact, etc.).

Take a common estimate for a very large investment by AI standards (GPT-3) - $12M. Multiple by 10x, and you're about halfway to the budget of the movie Tangled. 

JK Rowling made more $ off of Harry Potter books than the US gov't spends on AI over the course of a few years. Etc.

While AI research has gotten more capital-intensive in recent years, it's worth keeping this in perspective: AI spending remains tiny as a fraction of the economy. We're still in very early days compared to what's possible/likely eventually.
